note_sections.t: Review requested after an earlier positive prostate biopsy and a recent PSA increase to 7.3 ng/mL.

Mr X, a 65-year-old retired postal worker, initially entered the diagnostic pathway in May 2022 after a PSA rise triggered a positive biopsy revealing ISUP group 2 disease. Subsequent readings climbed from 4.3 ng/mL to 4.9 ng/mL by September 2023, peaking at 7.3 ng/mL in January 2025. He is married and shares a home with his partner. Lower urinary tract symptoms are moderate, scoring 13 on the IPSS questionnaire, mainly due to nocturia and a diminished urinary stream, yet he denies pelvic discomfort or visible blood in the urine. Ex-smoker (31 pack-yr, quit 2003), he maintains a daily 45-minute walking habit, consumes roughly two alcoholic drinks weekly, and recently received his annual influenza shot. He remains engaged with a local gardening club and handles his own financial matters without assistance. Comorbidities: none. Active medication: None.

DRE: The digital rectal examination is clinically normal. The prostate feels symmetrically enlarged at roughly 64 mL, presenting a smooth capsule without discrete nodules or focal asymmetry. Systemic assessment shows stable vital signs, including a blood pressure reading of 116/89 mmHg and a regular pulse at 66 beats per minute. The general physical survey reveals no abdominal masses or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
